topic: GPT-5.6 Sol Pricing Cut 50% on OpenRouter
summary: The headline 'GPT-5.6 Sol Pricing Cut 50% on OpenRouter' is literally true of what the OpenRouter model page displays, but wrong about who cut what. There were three separate price events in five days in August 2026, and only one of them was OpenAI repricing its own model. (1) Aug 17: OpenRouter put a 50% discount on GPT-5.6 Sol's OpenAI route -- non-BYOK traffic only, OpenAI provider only, announced to expire Sep 18. That is a channel promotion, not a vendor repricing; Azure and Bedrock did not follow. (2) Aug 21-22: OpenAI made a genuine, official cut to its own list price, $5/$30 -> $4/$20 per 1M short-context tokens (20% off input, 33% off output), stated as 'promotional pricing available at least through November 21, 2026' on OpenAI's own pricing and model pages. (3) Because OpenRouter's discount rides on top of the base rate, the 50% badge did not disappear when the base moved -- the number under it did: the Aug 17 promo was $2.50/$15, and as of today the same 50%-off route reads $2/$10. So the useful, checkable version of the story is: Sol's effective standard price has fallen from $5/$30 to $2/$10 on OpenRouter's OpenAI route in about five weeks, while the same model costs $4/$20 direct from OpenAI, $4/$20 on Azure, and $4.40/$22 on Bedrock in us-east-1 -- a 2.2x spread across endpoints for identical weights. Two traps silently eat most of that discount: the 272K long-context cliff (any prompt over 272,000 input tokens is billed at 2x input and 1.5x output for the entire request, so context-stuffing pays list price) and reasoning tokens, which bill at the output rate (6x-10x input) and scale with reasoning_effort. Finally, the per-token story is not the decision: OpenRouter processed roughly 1.59T GPT-5.6 Sol tokens in the last 7 days (~253B tokens/day across September, Sept 30 alone was 267B prompt + 3.5B completion = $196,653 of usage), but independent benchmark work puts Sol at $1.23 per Artificial Analysis Intelligence task versus Grok 4.6 at $0.84, and $8.37 per DeepSWE rollout versus Kimi K3's $4.65 with 14.7 solves per $100 against Sol's 5.3.

competitors.title: OpenRouter - GPT-5.6 Sol model page (PRIMARY, live 2026-10-01)
key_points: Page displays '50% off' next to '$2 / $10 per 1M' for the OpenAI route. Released Jul 9, 2026; knowledge cutoff Feb 16, 2026; 1,050,000-token context; 128,000 max output.
Ranked card on the page: 1.59T tokens processed in the last 7 days (as of Oct 1, 2026).

Per-provider table shows 7 endpoints with wildly different rates -- OpenAI Flex 50% off, OpenAI 50% off, OpenAI Fast 50% off, Azure, Azure (US), Azure (EU), Amazon Bedrock (US). Azure/Bedrock carry no discount.

OpenRouter's own explanatory copy on the page: 'The average price customers actually pay for this model, next to the prices providers post. Caching and discounts mean the price actually paid is often well below the listed one.'

Embedded daily usage series (standard variant) for September 2026 is present in page data: ~155B-380B prompt tokens/day and 1.7B-5.6B completion tokens/day; Sept 30 = 267.2B prompt + 3.5B completion, total_usage $196,653.52.

key_points: Flagship table has moved on to gpt-6.1-sol ($2/$10 standard) and gpt-6-astra ($10/$50), confirming GPT-5.6 Sol is no longer OpenAI's frontier model -- it now appears under a legacy 'Cyber models'/'All models' block at $4.00 input / $0.40 cached / $5.00 cache write / $20.00 output short-context, doubling to $8/$0.80/$10/$30 above 272K.

competitors.title: OpenRouter - GPT 5.6 Discounts & Jevons Paradox (Aug 25, 2026, updated Aug 27)
key_points: The original Terra/Luna discount ran Jul 27 - Aug 14, 2026. Daily Terra token usage rose 5.6x; daily Luna usage jumped 13.8x; 'The Sol model, which remained a list price, saw only a gentle bump of 1.1x over the same period.'
Terra/Luna went from 0.7% to 7.8% of all OpenRouter tokens, +7.1 share points; 'roughly three quarters of the gain came from outside OpenAI' (competitors gave up 5.3 points, other OpenAI models 1.9).

Retention: of 100K+ customers with Terra/Luna usage during the program, about 32% kept some usage afterwards and 18% ran at or above program pace; post-program daily Terra/Luna token volume was 1.38x the discount period.

Sol averaged 79.1B tokens/day during the Terra/Luna program against 71.2B/day pre-period -- an effectively flat control group. 'However, the shaded region in the chart above from Aug 17 onward is Sol's own 50% discount. Sol jumps immediately, reproducing the Terra/Luna pattern.' No final Sol multiplier was published.

Caveat stated by OpenRouter: 'Jul 30: OpenAI cut its own list prices (Luna 80%, Terra 20%) on top of the 50% discount through OpenRouter. As such, effective discounts from Jul 30 were Luna 90% and Terra 60%.'

competitors.title: AI Pricing Guru - OpenRouter Cuts GPT-5.6 Sol Price 50% (Aug 18, updated Aug 22, 2026)
key_points: Dated snapshot of the Aug 17 event: 'GPT-5.6 Sol OpenRouter -> OpenAI Standard: $5.00 / $0.5 / $30.00 -> $2.50 / $0.25 / $15.00, 50% all token categories.'

August 22 update: 'OpenAI has now made a separate direct-API cut to $4 input and $20 output per 1M short-context tokens. OpenRouter's eligible Standard route moved with that base rate and now shows $2 input, $0.20 cached input, $2.50 cache write, and $10 output.'
'Its endpoints API marks each OpenAI service tier with the same 50% discount, while Azure and Amazon Bedrock remain undiscounted.'

Web-search charges are separate and did not receive the token discount; the long-context tier above 272,000 input tokens is discounted too, so at promo rates long-context reads $5/$22.50 against $4/$20 direct.

competitors.title: explainx.ai - GPT-5.6 Sol Is Not 50% Cheaper, OpenRouter Is Just Running a Promo (Aug 18, 2026)
key_points: States the correction plainly: 'Did OpenAI cut GPT-5.6 Sol's price by 50%? No -- OpenAI's own listed price for Sol is unchanged. What's actually discounted? OpenRouter's non-BYOK rate for Sol.'

Attributes the mechanism to HN commenter wahnfrieden: 'OpenAI didn't cut the price of Sol by 50% like they did with Luna's 80%. Sol was unchanged. This is just a limited promo for OpenRouter non-BYOK.'
Points at the asymmetry as the tell: Luna's ~80% cut was announced by OpenAI and appears on OpenAI's own docs; Sol's 50% does not.
Also flags the practical constraint that no universal Zero Data Retention exists on OpenRouter.

competitors.title: Magic Tools - GPT-5.6 Sol's 50% Off Expires September 18 and Excludes BYOK (Aug 19, 2026)
key_points: Pulled from OpenRouter's public API on 2026-08-19 00:50 UTC: promo Input $2.50, Output $15.00, Cache read $0.25, Batch/Flex $1.25/$7.50, long-context $5.00/$22.50, web search $10/1000 calls undiscounted.
Effective 2026-08-17 (announcement tweet timestamped 17:36 UTC); expiring 2026-09-18; scope 'OpenRouter + Vercel AI Gateway only; requests routed to the OpenAI provider only; non-BYOK requests only.'

Trap one documented: the 272K pricing cliff -- above 272,000 input tokens input doubles to $5 and output rises to $22.50, i.e. undiscounted list, so 'stuff the whole codebase in' workloads see the promo as largely irrelevant.
Trap two: reasoning tokens bill at the output rate, so raising effort costs non-linearly.

Explains why provider pinning matters: 'The default Balanced routing usually lands on the discounted tier, but the safe move is to specify provider: {order: ["openai"]} explicitly. This one model has 3 providers and 7 endpoints on OpenRouter, priced anywhere from $2.50 to $5.50.'

competitors.title: Startup Fortune - OpenAI's Price Cut On GPT-5.6 Sol Sent OpenRouter Usage Up Nearly 14 Times (Aug 29, 2026)
key_points: Directly debunks the usage headline: 'the nearly 14-fold usage jump belongs to Luna, not Sol. OpenRouter's own August 25 analysis says the 13.8-times surge came from GPT-5.6 Luna during an earlier discount window, while Terra rose 5.6 times and Sol, then still at list price, moved only 1.1 times.'

Timeline: Aug 17 OpenRouter puts Sol on sale $5->$2.50 / $30->$15; Vercel AI Gateway posts a similar one-month 50% discount through September 18 for directly billed (non-BYOK) traffic; then 'OpenAI cut Sol's own list price on August 21, bringing its API price to $4 input and $20 output per million tokens for at least three months.'

On the incentive question: SemiAnalysis argued OpenRouter and Vercel are 'small pieces of OpenAI's total token volume but unusually important public data sources for estimating model share,' so halving prices there can inflate perceived demand.
Competitive context: Yahoo Finance citing GuruFocus reported Chinese AI models had captured 63% of U.S. OpenRouter usage.

competitors.title: Together AI - Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 Sol on DeepSWE: Cost, Coding, and Routing
key_points: DeepSWE pass@1: Sol 72.7% vs Kimi K3 68.5%; but pass@4 flips it -- K3 89.4% vs Sol 85.8%, and K3's coverage (tasks solved at least once across four tries) is 89.4% against Sol's 85.8%.
Cost per rollout: Sol $8.37 vs Kimi K3 $4.65. 'Solved tasks per $100: Kimi K3 14.7 vs GPT-5.6 Sol 5.3' -- about 2.8x the work per dollar.
Reliability axis favors Sol: 84.5% four-for-four pass rate with 61 rock-solid tasks vs K3's 76.6% and 45.

The models fail differently (0.46 per-task correlation), so a Kimi-first cascade that escalates to Sol reaches ~85.6% and covers 108 of 113 tasks -- better than either model alone or even a perfect one-shot router (83.4%).
Median rollout time: Sol 17 minutes vs K3 66 minutes; Sol uses roughly 40% fewer steps.

competitors.title: The Batch (DeepLearning.AI) - Grok 4.6 Rivals Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol at a Lower Cost Per Task
key_points: On Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, Grok 4.6 (high) ties GPT-5.6 Sol (max) at 61, but 'GPT-5.6 Sol set to max reasoning ($1.23 per task)' against Grok 4.6's $0.84 per task.
Claude Fable 5 (max, fallback) sits at 62 but costs $3.14 per task; Kimi K3 (max) at 60 for $0.84.
On Terminal-Bench 2.1: GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh 89.5%, Claude Opus 5 max 89.1%, Grok 4.6 88.4%.
Framing worth reusing: 'At the same price per token and task, an agent that finishes in half the turns costs around half as much.'

competitors.title: OpenRouter - OpenRouter is Joining Stripe (Aug 19, 2026)
key_points: Announced two days after the Sol promo went live, which is why the timing theory keeps coming up. OpenRouter: 'We now process 10+ trillion tokens per day from 400+ AI models for a community of over 10 million developers and companies.'
Commitment language: 'same mission, same name, same product, same roadmap... Routing decisions will remain driven by one thing: what's best for you, the user.'
Explicitly does not mention the GPT-5.6 Sol promotion. The promo's expiry (Sep 18) and the acquisition's announcement are correlated in time but the causal link is unconfirmed by any primary source.

Because the router discount rides on the provider's base rate, the 50% badge survived the price cut but the number under it changed: $2.50/$15 at launch of the promo, $2.00/$10.00 today.

Same weights, 4.4x spread between cheapest and dearest input.
The batch route openai/gpt-5.6-sol:batch lists $1.00 input / $5.00 output per 1M with a 50% discount flag -- five times cheaper per output token than OpenAI Fast on the same model.

Prompts over 272,000 input tokens are billed at 2x input and 1.5x output for the entire request on OpenAI's own rate card, and at $5.00/$22.50 on the discounted OpenRouter long-context tier -- i.e. at or above undiscounted list. Cache writes bill at 1.25x the uncached input rate.

OpenRouter processed 1.59T GPT-5.6 Sol tokens in the 7 days ending Oct 1, 2026, and ran at roughly 253B tokens/day across September (Sept 30 alone: 267.2B prompt + 3.5B completion tokens, $196,653 of metered usage).
stats.source: https://openrouter.ai/collections/discounted-models (7-day token counter, fetched 2026-10-01); daily series embedded in https://openrouter.ai/openai/gpt-5.6-sol page data (31 daily records, Sep 1 - Oct 1)

stats.fact: The celebrated 13.8x traffic surge belongs to Luna, not Sol. During the Jul 27-Aug 14 Terra/Luna discount, Luna rose 13.8x, Terra 5.6x, and Sol -- still at list -- rose only 1.1x, from 71.2B to 79.1B tokens/day. Sol's own 50% discount began Aug 17 and OpenRouter said it 'jumps immediately' but published no multiplier.
OpenAI's July 30 cut was a real repricing: Luna -80% ($1/$6 -> $0.20/$1.20) and Terra -20% ($2.50/$15 -> $2/$12). Sol did not move at all in that round.

Per-token savings are not the same as per-task savings: on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, GPT-5.6 Sol (max) costs $1.23 per task against Grok 4.6 (high) at $0.84 and Kimi K3 (max) at $0.84, while Claude Fable 5 (max) costs $3.14.

On DeepSWE, Sol costs $8.37 per rollout against Kimi K3's $4.65, and delivers 5.3 solved tasks per $100 versus K3's 14.7 -- but Sol is more reliable, posting an 84.5% four-for-four pass rate against K3's 76.6%.

OpenRouter adds no per-token markup but charges 5.5% on card credit purchases ($0.80 minimum) or 5% on crypto, so the real saving versus paying OpenAI directly is roughly 47%, not 50%. BYOK traffic bills at list price and forfeits the discount entirely, though BYOK carries its own free allowance ($25,000/month of list-price usage on pay-as-you-go).

The bare gpt-5.6 model alias routes to Sol, so leaving a model string unqualified bills at flagship rates by default while Terra or Luna may be sufficient -- the single most expensive default in the family.

stats.fact: GPT-5.6 Sol is no longer OpenAI's frontier model: gpt-6.1-sol sits at $2/$10 standard and gpt-6-astra at $10/$50 on OpenAI's own flagship table, which is the context in which a '50% cut' to a now-previous-generation model should be read.
stats.source: https://platform.openai.com/docs/pricing (live 2026-10-01); OpenRouter catalog shows openai/gpt-6.1-sol created 2026-09-29 and openai/gpt-6-astra at $10/$50

stats.fact: OpenRouter is being acquired by Stripe (announced Aug 19, 2026, two days after the Sol promo), and processes 10+ trillion tokens/day across 400+ models for 10M+ developers; the acquisition announcement contains no mention of the Sol promotion.

SemiAnalysis argued the discount's real function may be scoreboard management: OpenRouter and Vercel are a small share of OpenAI's volume but the main public data source used to estimate model share, so halving prices there is cheap and visibly doubles Sol's volume on the charts people use to judge OpenAI against Anthropic.

At the original promo rate Sol's cache read was $0.25/1M (50% off the $0.50 list) and today's discounted cache read is $0.20/1M against OpenAI's direct $0.40 -- caching is where the discount compounds, since agent sessions run roughly 20:1 input to output.

angles: CORRECTION-FIRST HOOK: 'GPT-5.6 Sol's price was cut 50%' is the version that spread (636 points, 449 comments on HN on Aug 17-18). The accurate version is better: OpenRouter ran a non-BYOK, OpenAI-route-only promo starting Aug 17, OpenAI independently cut its own list price $5/$30 -> $4/$20 on Aug 21, and because the promo percentage sits on top of the base rate, the same 50% badge now reads $2/$10. Readers get a concrete, checkable correction plus something they can act on.

THE BADGE OUTLIVED ITS NUMBER: most coverage froze at $2.50/$15 (the Aug 17 snapshot). Today's live endpoints API returns $2.00/$10.00 for the same 50%-off badge. Showing the snapshot vs live delta demonstrates the article is verified rather than aggregated, and explains why a promo 'expiring Sep 18' is still visible in October -- the expiry applied to the promo, not to the badge, which re-based when OpenAI moved its list price.

ONE MODEL, SEVEN ENDPOINTS, FOUR PRICES: $1/$5 (Flex) to $4.40/$22 (Bedrock/Azure-EU) for identical weights -- a 4.4x spread on input. The decision is not 'which model' but 'which route, which tier, which provider tag'. Include the exact provider-pinning snippet (provider.order) and warn that default Balanced routing may or may not land on the discounted endpoint.

THE TWO TRAPS THAT EAT THE DISCOUNT: (a) the 272K cliff -- any prompt over 272,000 input tokens bills at 2x input / 1.5x output for the whole request, so long-context workloads pay list price and the promo is nearly irrelevant; (b) reasoning tokens bill at output rates and scale with reasoning_effort, so a task that looks cheap per token is not. This is the section that saves readers money and nobody writes it.

USAGE-REALITY CHECK: Sol's 7-day volume on OpenRouter is 1.59T tokens (~253B/day in September, $196K on Sept 30 alone) -- the promotion demonstrably coincided with a step change, but the famous 13.8x multiplier belongs to Luna, and Sol was measured at just 1.1x while it was the control group. Pair that with SemiAnalysis's incentive critique so readers can read router scoreboards correctly.

COST PER RESOLVED TASK, NOT PER TOKEN: Sol at $1.23/task vs Grok 4.6 at $0.84 on AA; $8.37/rollout vs Kimi K3's $4.65 on DeepSWE with 14.7 vs 5.3 solves per $100 -- yet Sol has the higher four-for-four reliability (84.5% vs 76.6%) and costs less per resolved issue than Grok 4.6 on SWE-Bench Pro because it burns fewer steps. The price cut makes Sol a value pick for hard work, not a blanket default.

STRATEGIC WHY: Sol is no longer OpenAI's frontier (GPT-6 Astra is, at $10/$50; GPT-6.1 Sol at $2/$10), Chinese open-weight models reportedly hold a large share of US OpenRouter usage, and OpenRouter just agreed to be acquired by Stripe. Read the '50% cut' as a legacy-flagship repositioning plus a scoreboard-visible demand lever, not as a frontier price war.

MIGRATION/BUDGET GUIDANCE: pin the endpoint, hold context under 272K, reuse cached prefixes (cache read is a tenth of input), move non-urgent work to batch ($1/$5), and choose deliberately between discounted non-BYOK routing and BYOK (free under $25k/month of list-price usage but no promo). Budget against $4/$20 direct as the planning number and treat $2/$10 as upside with a known end date.

TONE NOTE: avoid 'OpenAI slashed prices' framing; OpenAI's own number is a >20% promotional reduction with a stated end date, and the router number is a channel promotion. Both are real; conflating them is what made the original headline wrong. The honest version is more useful because it gives readers two separate levers to pull.

editorial_notes: Every price in the article must be dated and attributed to a specific surface (OpenAI docs vs OpenRouter endpoints API vs Azure vs Bedrock). The single biggest failure mode in the competing coverage is attaching a router promo price to OpenAI's rate card, or vice versa -- explainx.ai and cooconsbit both had to add correction sections because of it.

The Nov 21, 2026 end date (OpenAI's own) and the Sep 18, 2026 end date (OpenRouter's original promo window) are different promises on different layers. State both and note that as of Oct 1 the OpenRouter discount is still displaying, so the Sep 18 expiry evidently did not simply turn the badge off.

The 50% badge is on the OpenAI provider tag only. Azure and Bedrock endpoints for the same model return discount=0 in the live API. If the article claims 'Sol is half price on OpenRouter', qualify it to the OpenAI route in the same sentence.
Avoid citing the 13.8x usage figure next to Sol; it is Luna's number from the earlier discount window and misattributing it is the exact error the original coverage made and later corrected.

The OpenRouter rankings page embeds an Artificial Analysis score column that shows GPT-5.6 Sol (max) at 50.2 while AA's own published comparisons put Sol (max) at 59-61 -- index re-baselining, not a regression. If quoting benchmark numbers, cite the dated source and note the index version, or prefer the per-task cost figures which are more stable and more decision-relevant.

Do not repeat unverified acquisition-theory causation (Stripe timing -> promo). OpenRouter's Stripe post does not mention the promotion; present the timing as observed correlation and label the SemiAnalysis reading as third-party analysis, as cooconsbit correctly does.
open_questions: OpenRouter never published a final Sol multiplier for the Aug 17 discount (only 'Sol jumps immediately'), so the size of Sol's own demand response is unquantified by the platform itself.

Whether the OpenRouter discount persists past its original Sep 18 window was not restated in any primary source retrieved; the badge was still live in the Oct 1 endpoints API, which is evidence but not a policy statement.
OpenAI has not disclosed what rates apply after the Nov 21, 2026 promotional period, so any long-run cost model should treat $4/$20 as a window, not a list price.
